title: Why AI Agents Need an Ontology: The Write Path Nobody Talks About (2026)
summary: AI agents fail at the write boundary, not in the model. Learn what an ontology is, why validate-before-commit beats a bigger model, and how to skip the build.
body_markdown:
In the 1930s, a Bell Labs engineer named Phillip H. Smith had a problem that looked like bad luck and turned out to be geometry.


He was testing antenna arrays fed by long transmission lines, and when he pushed power down a line, a large part of it came straight back at him. The signal was not being absorbed, blocked, or stolen. It was **reflecting** , and the reason was simple once he could see it: at the point where the line met the antenna, an electrical property changed. Waves do not care about obstacles. They reflect at **discontinuities** .


Smith's fix was not a bigger transmitter. It was a new way of drawing the problem. He had a polar version by 1936, refined it into its final form in early 1937, and[published it in Electronics magazine in January 1939](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smith_chart) . The idea was apparently so overdue that two other engineers reached it independently: Tōsaku Mizuhashi in Japan, published December 1937, and Amiel R. Volpert in the Soviet Union, developed in 1939 and published in February 1940. It is still called the Volpert diagram in Russian and, by some Japanese engineers, the Mizuhashi chart.


The chart is still printed, still taught, and still built into radio test equipment almost ninety years later. And the lesson underneath it is the one every AI agent team in 2026 is quietly re-learning.


> **TL;DR:** AI agents mostly fail at the boundary where a probabilistic guess meets a deterministic system that expects exact IDs, exact field names, and exact allowed values. An ontology is the shared agreement that makes that boundary checkable, and it does not need a six-month modeling project.[Taskade Genesis](https://www.taskade.com/create?entry_kind=content&source=blog&entry=%2Fblog%2Fagent-ontology-explained) generates the structure, the agents, and the automations together.


---


## Why Do AI Agents Fail in Production?


AI agents fail most often at the **write boundary** , not inside the model. The model produces a plausible proposal, and the system on the other side needs an exact record ID, an allowed status value, and a field that actually exists. When those two things disagree, the work bounces back as a retry, a corrupted record, or a silent wrong answer that nobody catches until a customer does.


This is worth stating plainly because the industry keeps proposing the wrong fix. When an agent misbehaves, the reflex is to reach for a larger model, a longer context window, or another paragraph of prompt. Those interventions change how good the guess is. They do not change what happens when a good guess meets a system that will accept anything it is handed.


Gartner predicted in June 2025 that[more than 40% of agentic AI projects would be canceled by the end of 2027](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-06-25-gartner-predicts-over-40-percent-of-agentic-ai-projects-will-be-canceled-by-end-of-2027) . That figure gets repeated constantly. The release does cite a January 2025 poll of 3,412 webinar attendees on investment posture, but it publishes no derivation for the 40% figure itself. Treat it as a directional prediction rather than a measurement. The more useful evidence is architectural, and it points at the same place every time: the failures cluster at handoffs.


A retry sends the work back to the model, and the same boundary waits for the next proposal.


Smith's insight transfers exactly. **Reflection is caused by a discontinuity, not by an obstruction.** Nothing is blocking your agent. Something changes across the seam, and the work comes back.


Anthropic's engineering team named the same seam precisely when writing about tool design in September 2025: tools are *"a new kind of software which reflects a contract between deterministic systems and non-deterministic agents."* A contract is exactly the right word, and it is the thing most agent stacks never write down.


The reason boundaries dominate agent failure rather than merely contributing to it is arithmetic. Chip Huyen laid it out in January 2025: at **95% accuracy per step** , a ten-step task lands at **60%** , and a hundred-step task at **0.6%** . Per-step accuracy is what a better model buys you. Step count is what an agent adds. When those multiply, small boundary errors stop being annoyances and become the dominant term.


Per-step accuracy 5 steps 10 steps 20 steps


90% 59% 35% 12%


95% 77% 60% 36%


99% 95% 90% 82%


The table explains why teams keep being surprised. Moving a model from 90% to 95% per step feels incremental in a benchmark and nearly triples a twenty-step task's success rate. It also explains the ceiling: you cannot reach reliable long-horizon work by improving the per-step number alone, because the exponent is doing more work than the base.


---


## What Is an Ontology in AI?


An ontology is an explicit, shared agreement about what things exist in a domain, what is true about each of them, and how they relate to each other. The standard definition comes from Stanford computer scientist Tom Gruber, in a paper published in *Knowledge Acquisition* in 1993: **"An ontology is an explicit specification of a conceptualization."**


The sentence before it is the one that matters more for agents, and it is almost never quoted: *"Every knowledge base, knowledge-based system, or knowledge-level agent is committed to some conceptualization, explicitly or implicitly."* Gruber's point was that the commitment exists either way. The only choice is whether it is written down where something can check it. Rudi Studer and colleagues tightened the definition in 1998 by adding two words that carry most of the weight: a **formal, explicit** specification of a **shared** conceptualization.


Stripped of the philosophy, an ontology for AI agents answers five questions:


Element Question it answers Concrete example


**Things** What does the system need to remember? Customer, Order, Invoice, Ticket


**Facts** What must be known about each thing? An Order has a status, a total, a created date


**Links** How do things relate? Every Order references exactly one Customer


**Rules** What must be true? An Order cannot ship before payment clears


**Change** What enters, moves, or becomes different? Draft to Paid to Shipped, never Draft to Shipped


That is the entire concept. Everything else in this field is an argument about notation.


### Ontology vs Taxonomy vs Schema vs Knowledge Graph vs Semantic Layer


These five words get used interchangeably by people selling five different products. They are not the same thing, and knowing the difference is the fastest way to work out what you actually need.


Term What it is What it does NOT do


**Taxonomy** A hierarchy of categories, parent to child Say nothing about relationships between branches, or about rules


**Schema** The field and type definition for one store Carry meaning across systems, or express cross-entity rules


**Ontology** Entities, properties, relationships, and constraints, shared across systems Store the actual records


**Knowledge graph** The populated data: real nodes and real edges Guarantee consistency unless an ontology constrains it


**Semantic layer** Governed metric and dimension definitions for queries Usually cover the write path or permitted actions


The one-line version: **the ontology is the agreement, the knowledge graph is the data, and the semantic layer is the read-path slice of the agreement.** If you want the storage half of this story in depth, we covered it separately in[how AI agents use knowledge graphs](https://www.taskade.com/blog/knowledge-graph-agents) . This article is about the half nobody writes about.


### Do You Need OWL, RDF, and SHACL?


Probably not, and the reason why is the most useful thing in this section. These three W3C standards get named in almost every ontology article and almost never explained, which leaves readers assuming they are a package deal. They are not.


Standard Status in 2026 What it is for


**RDF** 1.1 is a Recommendation from 2014; RDF 1.2 reached Candidate Recommendation in April 2026 A data model: everything is a subject, predicate, object triple


**OWL** Recommendation since 2009, second edition 2012, **unchanged since** A logic for stating what *follows* from what


**SHACL** Recommendation since July 2017; a 1.2 revision is in Working Draft A language for **validating** a graph against shapes and reporting violations


**ShEx** Community Group report, stalled at 2.1 in 2019, **never a W3C Recommendation** A competing validation language with a compact grammar


The detail that matters for agents is the difference between the middle two rows, and it is the single most common confusion in this field.


**OWL is a reasoner, not a validator.** It operates under what the W3C's own primer calls the open-world assumption: *"If some fact is not present in a database, it is usually considered false (the so-called closed-world assumption) whereas in the case of an OWL 2 document it may simply be missing (but possibly true)."* OWL also makes no unique-name assumption, so two different identifiers may quietly refer to the same thing.


Read that again with an agent in mind. If you hand an under-specified record to an OWL reasoner, **it does not complain. It infers.** A missing required field is not an error; it is an unknown. That is exactly the wrong behavior at a write boundary, and it is why using OWL as a guard is a category error rather than a configuration mistake.


SHACL exists to fill that gap. It validates a given graph against shapes, and returns a report where` sh:conforms` is true only if validation produced no results at all. Its constraint vocabulary is the checklist a write boundary actually needs:` sh:class` and` sh:datatype` for types,` sh:minCount` and` sh:maxCount` for cardinality,` sh:pattern` for format,` sh:node` to require conformance to another shape, and` sh:closed` to reject any property the shape does not explicitly allow.


There is a quiet signal in that table worth noticing. **OWL has not changed since 2012, while validation has kept moving.** The field's center of gravity shifted from inferring what must be true to checking what is being claimed, which is precisely the shift this article is arguing for.


You can adopt all of that thinking without adopting any of the syntax. A JSON Schema on a tool call, a Pydantic model, or a typed field with fixed options enforces the same four checks. The standards are one notation for the idea. **The idea is what you need.**


---


## What Is the Impedance Mismatch Between Agents and Systems?


Software already has a name for this class of problem. The **object-relational impedance mismatch** describes the friction between an object model and a relational database, and Ted Neward's 2006 essay[The Vietnam of Computer Science](https://blogs.newardassociates.com/blog/2006/the-vietnam-of-computer-science.html) is its most quoted diagnosis: a quagmire that "starts well, gets more complicated as time passes, and before long entraps its users in a commitment that has no clear demarcation point, no clear win conditions, and no clear exit strategy."


The phrase has already been pointed at AI systems by several people, so this is not a new label. What has not been carried across is the **engineering discipline that came with it** . In radio, the mismatch is not a metaphor for friction. It is a measurable quantity with a known fix, and the fix has rules.


The first rule is that matching requires two quantities to resolve together, not one. Resistances must be equal, and reactances equal and opposite, so the phases cancel rather than merely agree:


- **Magnitude** is how big the effect is. In agent terms, capability. Can the model do the task at all?
- **Phase** is *when* it happens relative to everything else. In agent terms, ordering. Does the information arrive before the decision that depends on it?


Matching magnitude alone does not work. You can force the numbers to agree by adding a resistor, and **the power actually delivered gets worse** , because a resistor matches by burning the mismatch as heat while the timing stays wrong.


This is the single most useful thing to carry into agent design. A capable model with the wrong ordering produces work that is beautifully executed and wrong, which is a failure that survives every quality review because nothing about it looks broken.


Mismatch type Electrical analogue What it looks like in an agent


**Magnitude** Resistance differs across the seam Model genuinely cannot do the task


**Phase** Reactance shifts the timing Model acts before it has the record it needs


**Total reflection** Open or short circuit Agent asks endlessly, or writes without checking anything


**Lossy line** Attenuation flatters the meter Looks clean because it barely produced anything


That last row is the trap in every agent evaluation. A line long enough to absorb its own reflections reads as a perfect match at the input while delivering nothing at the far end. An agent that emits three files instead of twelve will post excellent error rates. **Never report a quality ratio without also reporting how much got done.**


*Image: Bare Bones Smith Chart by Hula Hula Hula,[Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bare_Bones_Smith_Chart_-_with_annotations.png) , CC0.*


The chart above is the artifact Smith produced, and its design contains one more idea worth stealing. It folds an **infinite** space, every possible impedance from a dead short to an open circuit, into a **finite** disk, using a Möbius transformation. The center is a perfect match. Distance from the center is how much of your signal is coming back.


Smith did not make the problem smaller. He changed the coordinates until the answer became a position you could point at. That is what a good ontology does to a domain: it does not reduce what your business contains, it makes the part an agent must respect small enough to check.


### The evidence that representation is itself a failure mode


If the shape of the agreement at the boundary were a minor implementation detail, changing it would barely move results. It does not barely move results.


The[Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard](https://gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/leaderboard.html) has a[format sensitivity test](https://gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/blogs/17_bfcl_v4_prompt_variation.html) that measures the same models on the same tool-calling tasks while varying only **how the tools are described** and how results come back: documentation as Python, XML or JSON, tool-call tags on or off, plain text versus markdown. Across 26 prompt variations, the gap between the best and worst representation of an identical task reaches **81.5 percentage points** in the leaderboard's published data. One model swings from 79% to **0%** on the same work, purely on notation.


One caveat stated plainly, because it matters: that spread is measured for models being *prompted* to call tools, not for native function-calling APIs, which are more stable. It is not a claim that your production stack will swing 80 points. It is evidence for something narrower and more important: **the representation at the boundary is not neutral packaging. It is part of the system's behavior.**


Even at the top of that leaderboard (as updated in April 2026), nothing exceeds roughly 77% overall accuracy, and the sub-scores say where the trouble is. In the multi-turn tests, the best model handles a well-formed request at 81% and a **missing parameter at 58%** . The hardest thing in tool use is not doing the task. It is behaving correctly when the information does not fit the expected shape, which is the definition of a boundary failure.


---


## Why Read-Path Ontology Is Solved and the Write Path Is Not


Almost every article about ontologies and AI agents is about **reading** : ground the agent in better context so it retrieves the right thing and hallucinates less. That work is genuinely mature. Retrieval, graph memory, and semantic layers all serve it well.


The write path is where the money is lost, and it is nearly unwritten. Here is the difference, and it is not subtle.


A wrong read produces a bad sentence. A wrong write produces a refunded order that should not have been refunded, an email to the wrong client, or a record whose customer ID points at nothing. You can regenerate a sentence. You cannot un-send the email.


The asymmetry has a name in the 2026 literature. Enterprise agent systems constrain agent **inputs** heavily, through context assembly, tool discovery, and governance thresholds, while leaving **outputs** essentially unchecked. A 2026 preprint,[Ontology-Constrained Neural Reasoning in Enterprise Agentic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00555) , calls this asymmetric neurosymbolic coupling and argues for extending the constraint to the output side.


The strongest empirical result available comes from an April 2026 preprint,[Bounded Autonomy for Enterprise AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14723) , with the caveats that it has not been peer reviewed and its authors evaluate their own bounded-autonomy layer across 25 scenarios. It frames unsafe agent behavior as an **execution architecture problem** rather than a model problem. In a deployed multi-tenant evaluation across seven failure families, constraining execution through typed action contracts with validation before side effects completed 23 of 25 scenarios with zero unsafe executions, against 17 of 25 for the unconstrained baseline.


Read that comparison carefully. Same models. Different boundary. Better outcomes and fewer disasters.


Gartner reached the same structure from the governance direction. In[a May 2026 release](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-05-26-gartner-says-applying-uniform-governance-across-ai-agents-will-lead-to-enterprise-ai-agent-failure) it predicted that by 2027, **40% of enterprises will demote or decommission autonomous AI agents** because of governance gaps "identified only after production incidents occur," and set out four autonomy levels:


Level What the agent may do What it implies


**1. Observe** Read only No boundary risk


**2. Advise** Read only, recommends actions Humans remain the write path


**3. Act with approval** Writes after explicit human approval per action Validate-before-commit, with a person as the validator


**4. Act autonomously** Writes independently Requires guardrails, rapid rollback, and circuit breakers


The interesting level is 3, and Gartner's own warning about it is the honest one: approvals "can degrade under time pressure or approval fatigue, creating a false sense of safety." A human clicking approve on every write is a validator that gets worse the more it is used. **That is precisely the argument for making the check mechanical** , and reserving the human for the cases the machine could not resolve.


The chart below shows the preprint's completion counts. The zero-unsafe-execution result applies to the bounded run.


The interesting part is not that the constrained system scored higher. It is that the constrained system scored higher **using the same models** . Nothing about the intelligence changed. Only what was allowed to reach the database.


---


## How Do You Validate an Agent's Output Before It Commits?


You separate **deciding** from **committing** . The agent's output stops being a command and becomes a proposal that has to pass a check before it changes anything.


Four steps, in order:


1. **Form** the intended change as structured data, not prose.
2. **Check** its types, values, references, and relationships against the ontology.
3. **Commit** only after it passes.
4. **Confirm** the resulting state from what the system returns, not from what the model believes it did.


Step 4 is the one teams skip. An agent that reports success because it *believes* the write worked is generating fiction about its own effects. The confirmation has to come from the tool response.


### What the validation actually checks


The check is not one thing. It is four, and they fail differently:


Check Question Typical failure it catches


**Shape** Do these fields exist, with these types? Model invents a field name


**Value** Is this within the allowed set? Status set to "done" when the options are Open, Closed


**Reference** Does this ID point at a real record? Fabricated customer ID


**Relationship** Is this link permitted between these types? Invoice attached to a Ticket instead of an Account


Shape and value checks are cheap and catch the majority of mechanical errors. **Reference checks are the ones that matter most** , because a fabricated ID is the failure that looks completely normal until something downstream tries to follow it.


Here is the pattern in plain, portable terms. Nothing here requires a graph database or a modeling language:


```text
PROPOSAL from agent
{
"action": "update_order_status",
"order_id": "ord_8812",
"status": "refunded",
"reason": "customer request"
}


VALIDATE against the ontology
shape        status is a field on Order .................. pass
value        "refunded" is in {open,paid,shipped,refunded}  pass
reference    ord_8812 exists ......................... pass
relationship Order.refund requires a paid predecessor .. FAIL


RESULT  rejected, returned to agent with the reason
"order ord_8812 is in state 'open'; refund requires 'paid'"


AGENT   repairs once, or escalates to a person


```


The rejection message matters as much as the rejection. An agent told only "invalid" retries blindly. An agent told **which rule failed and what the current state is** can usually fix it on the first attempt, which is the difference between one extra call and a loop.


Drawn as an interaction, the boundary sits between two participants who should never talk directly:


Notice that the agent never touches the system of record. Every arrow into it passes through the validator, which is the structural difference between a system that can be wrong and a system that can be corrupted.


### The wire format already exists


This is not theoretical plumbing you have to invent. The[Model Context Protocol](https://www.taskade.com/blog/mcp) specification updated in July 2026 lifted tool input and output schemas to full JSON Schema 2020-12, with composition, conditionals, and references. In practice that means **the ontology can ship as the tool schema itself** . The agreement about what a valid change looks like travels with the tool the agent is calling, rather than living in a document that someone hopes the prompt mentioned.


Both major model providers now enforce schemas mechanically rather than hopefully. OpenAI shipped Structured Outputs in August 2024; Anthropic shipped structured outputs and strict tool use in public beta in November 2025 and has since made them generally available. Both compile your schema into a grammar and mask invalid tokens during sampling, so a non-conforming response is not merely unlikely, it is unreachable.


The most revealing line in OpenAI's original announcement is one almost nobody quotes. Training the model to follow complex schemas got it to **93%** , and the post says plainly that this "still did not meet the reliability that developers need to build robust applications," so they added a deterministic constraint layer to reach 100%.


That gap is the entire argument of this article in one number. **Ninety-three percent is what better models buy you. The last seven points are what a boundary buys you.** No amount of additional training was going to close it, because the failure was not a knowledge problem.


---


## What Does an Ontology Check Catch That a Type Check Misses?


A type check confirms that a tool call has the right shape. An ontology check confirms that the result makes sense in your domain. A refund with a real order ID and a valid amount passes the first check and still fails the second when that order was already refunded. Agents need both gates.


Frank Coyle, who lectures at UC Berkeley, drew this split in his 2026 talk[Why Agentic Systems Need Ontologies](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Sir59K8ZDPU) . The model proposes a tool call, the application runs the tool, and a validator compares the result with the ontology. A reasonable result continues. An unreasonable one goes back to the model or to a person. A line from Frank Coyle's talk sums it up: **"Pydantic at the door, ontology at the ledger."** In his design, agents cause no side effects until the check passes.


Coyle's three examples are all writes that are well-formed and wrong:


Error Why a type check passes it Rule that states it Layer that rejects it


A second refund on the same order Order ID and amount are valid At most one refund per order (` owl:FunctionalProperty` )` sh:maxCount 1` , or an application check


A payout sent to the support rep instead of the buyer The payee is a real person ID Customer and support rep are disjoint classes (` owl:disjointWith` )` sh:class` on the payee, or a role check


An invented status such as "probably shipped" It is a string Status is one of paid, shipped, refunded (` owl:oneOf` )` sh:in` , an enum, or a fixed-option field


One correction belongs beside that table. The talk presents the OWL constructs as the guardrail, and OWL polices only some of them. A reasoner does flag the payout to a support rep, because one individual cannot belong to two disjoint classes. The duplicate refund is different. Under the open-world assumption covered earlier, a reasoner that sees two refunds on a functional property can conclude that the two refunds are the same individual, and no error is raised. The invented status has the same gap unless the allowed values are declared different from one another. For those cases the rejection has to come from a closed-world layer: SHACL shapes, a schema, or plain application code. State the rule once, then enforce it somewhere that can say no.


The same need appears in the field. The founders of Lassie, a company that automates insurance billing for dental offices, said in[an a16z interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Fpg_8aiBxx4) that they had to "build an ontology to make sure that everybody in this whole ecosystem is on the same page about an insurance claim and the patient payment," because each system they connect defines those terms a little differently. Until one definition of a claim exists, an agent can be right in one system and wrong in the next.


---


## What Does Structure Cost You?


Structure is not free, and the honest version of this argument has to say so. This is also the part of the debate most articles get wrong, so it is worth walking carefully.


The commonly cited evidence against constraining output is *Let Me Speak Freely?* (Tam et al., EMNLP 2024 Industry Track), which reported "a significant decline in LLMs' reasoning abilities under format restrictions." That sentence gets repeated everywhere as a settled result. **It is not settled, and the reason why is more useful than the headline.**


Buried in that same paper is a finding that explains most of its own result. Inspecting the failures, the authors found that **100% of one model's JSON-mode responses placed the` answer` key before the` reason` key** . The schema had ordered the fields so the model had to commit to an answer *before* writing its reasoning, which silently converted chain-of-thought prompting into direct answering. The reasoning did not degrade because tokens were masked. It degraded because **the shape asked for the conclusion first.**


That is the single most practical thing in this article:


> **Field order in your schema is not cosmetic. It is execution order.** Put` reasoning` before` answer` , and` evidence` before` decision` . A model fills fields in the order you declare them, so a schema that asks for the verdict first has removed the thinking that would have justified it.


Two other results point the same way. A[2026 study of 44 models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18476) found that answer diversity collapses when you *ask* for JSON in the prompt, while schema enforcement at the decoder "compresses no further than the request (-0.03 bits)." And the[JSONSchemaBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.10868) benchmark re-ran the disputed reasoning tasks across several constrained-decoding frameworks and found constrained decoding **beat** unconstrained generation on all three, concluding that "constrained decoding, regardless of the framework, achieves higher performance than the unconstrained setting." Read that one with its provenance in view: most of its authors are at Microsoft, which ships Guidance, the framework the paper rates best.


So where is the real cost? Two places, both about the constraint being wrong rather than present:


Claim Standing What it actually shows


Format restrictions hurt reasoning **Largely explained** Mostly schema field order destroying chain-of-thought


Structured generation is free **Vendor position** True for schema conformance, not for output quality


Greedy masking distorts the distribution **Real, peer reviewed** Valid outputs appear at likelihoods the model did not assign


An **incomplete** constrainer is dangerous **Real, measured** Rejecting valid outputs pushes generation into low-probability space


That last row is the one to take seriously. A 2026 study,[The Alignment Problem in Constrained Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21619) , found that when the constrainer rejects programs it should have allowed, functional correctness fell **by up to 97%** , because the model gets forced into regions it considers unlikely. Over-constraining is worse than not constraining. A validator that is wrong about what is valid does more damage than no validator at all.


And the honest ceiling, from a[2026 software-engineering study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09395) : its strictest template-driven control "nearly eliminates syntax errors, yet substantial structural and semantic errors persist." These tools are **necessary but insufficient.** They guarantee the shape. They never guarantee the content is true.


None of this argues against validation. It argues for putting the structure in the right place, and getting it right.


Where you constrain Effect on reasoning Verdict


The model's **thinking** Degrades it, per the EMNLP result Avoid


The **proposal** the model emits Minimal, if the schema is simple Good


The **commit** into your system None, it happens after reasoning ends Best


The rule that falls out: **let the agent think in prose and act in types.** Reasoning stays loose. The moment the work becomes a change to real state, it passes through a shape that can reject it. Constraining the write path costs nothing cognitively, because the cognition is already finished.


There are two other real costs worth naming. Validation adds a round trip on the failure path, so a rejected write costs one extra call plus a repair. And an ontology is a maintained artifact: it can drift from the system it describes, which is the failure mode that killed the previous generation of enterprise modeling projects. The second cost is the serious one, and it is the strongest argument for keeping the shape **inside** the product rather than beside it.


---


## The Resistor and the Stub: Two Kinds of Fix


Every fix you can apply to a misbehaving agent falls into one of two categories, and Smith's lab gives us the right names for them.


A **resistor** matches by dissipating energy. It works, it always costs, and the cost is permanent. A **stub** is Smith's other solution: a dead-end scrap of the *same cable* , connected to nothing, cut to a specific length and spliced into the line. It cancels the reflection by changing timing rather than by burning power. It costs the price of a piece of wire.


Intervention Type Why


Switch to a larger, costlier model Resistor Recurring cost per call; only helps if the deficit was capability


Add more context to every prompt Resistor Pays tokens on every request, forever


Retry on failure with no diagnosis Resistor Multiplies cost, changes nothing structural


Validate before commit **Stub** One check, catches the class permanently


Require IDs instead of names **Stub** Costs nothing, removes an entire failure family


Fix the order that steps run in **Stub** Pure sequencing, zero marginal cost


Return the failed rule in the error **Stub** One string, converts blind retries into repairs


Most teams reach for the top three because they are the easiest to buy. The bottom four are the ones that compound.


And the deepest part of the analogy is the one worth sitting with: **the stub is made of the same cable it is fixing.** The best ontology for your agents is not a separate artifact maintained beside your system. It is your system's own structure, made explicit enough to check against.


---


## Do You Have to Build an Ontology First?


No, and attempting the full version first is the most reliable way to kill the project. The multi-year enterprise modeling effort is a well-documented failure pattern: the committee moves slower than the domain, and by the time the model is ratified the business has changed underneath it.


What you need instead is what we would call a **domain shape** : the smallest description of the world that lets one real workflow close. Five lines, not five hundred.


The last step feeds the first. What real usage reveals goes back into the domain shape as an extension, and the cycle runs again.


The test for whether something belongs in the shape is not whether it exists in your business. It is whether **some agent or automation needs to act on it** . A Customer that no workflow touches is a noun, not an entity.


### Capability test, not resource checklist


There is a related trap on the build side. Teams specify their agent system as a shopping list, then measure completion by whether the list got built.


```text
CHECKLIST THINKING                CAPABILITY THINKING


"2 databases"                     Can it remember what matters?
"1 agent"                         Can it reason where reasoning helps?
"1 automation"                    Can it act where action helps?
"1 dashboard"                     Can a person see and change the result?


Produces: architecture            Produces: a working loop


```


A system built to satisfy counts produces scaffolding. A system built to close a loop produces something a person can use on the first day. Never create an entity, agent, or automation to satisfy a number.


---


## How Do You Keep Facts, Inference, and Policy Apart?


Most agent trust problems are really **category errors** : the system presents a guess as a stored fact, or hard-codes a business decision as though it were a law of nature.


Keeping five categories distinct costs nothing and prevents an entire class of confusion:


Category What it is Where it should live


**Fact** A stored observation A field on a record


**Relationship** A connection between records An explicit reference by ID


**Derived value** Deterministic result computed from facts Calculated at read time, never stored as fact


**Inference** The agent's interpretation Labeled as a suggestion, with its basis


**Policy** A decision the organization made and can change An editable rule, not buried in a prompt


The rule that follows: **an agent must never present inference as stored fact.** "This account looks at risk of churning" and "this account churned" are different claims, and a system that renders them identically has taught its users to distrust both.


The dotted path to "Unlabeled inference stored as fact" is the one to design against. Inference flowing back into the fact store without a label is how a workspace slowly fills with confident guesses that later readers, human and machine, treat as ground truth.


The policy row deserves emphasis. When a business rule is written into prose inside a prompt, nobody can inspect it, test it, or change it without editing the prompt and re-qualifying the agent. When it lives as an editable rule, it is visible, versionable, and changeable by the person who actually owns the decision.

## How Should You Bound an AI Agent Loop?


Give every loop a stop condition **before** you give it autonomy. A defensible default is one plan, one execution attempt, one corrective retry when validation fails, then a handoff to a person.


The instinct to let agents self-correct indefinitely is intuitive and wrong. In[Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798) , presented at ICLR 2024, Google DeepMind and UIUC researchers found that models "struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback, and at times, their performance even degrades after self-correction."


The numbers are blunt. Asked to review and revise its own answers with no external signal, GPT-4 on grade-school maths went **95.5% to 91.5% to 89.0%** across two rounds of self-correction, while consuming five model calls instead of one:


Rounds of self-correction Model calls GSM8K accuracy


None 1 **95.5%**


One 3 91.5%


Two 5 89.0%


Five times the cost for a **6.5 point drop** . The authors' explanation is that the model cannot judge the correctness of its own reasoning, so when it does change an answer it is more likely to break a right one than fix a wrong one. Self-correction is not free improvement with a cost attached. It is a coin flip with a cost attached.


Repetition is also the single most common way these systems fail in the wild. A 2025 Berkeley study,[Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657) , annotated failure traces across seven open-source multi-agent frameworks and found failure rates from 41% to 86.7%, with **step repetition the most frequent failure mode of all fourteen it catalogued at 15.7%** , reasoning-action mismatch second at 13.2%, and "unaware of termination conditions" third at 12.4%. The most common way multi-agent AI fails is by redoing what it already did.


Which is the entire argument for validation as the loop's exit condition. A retry driven by an external check that says *this specific rule failed, and here is the current state* is genuinely informative. A retry driven by "try again, think harder" is the failure mode the paper measured.


Frank Coyle, a longtime SMU computer science professor who now lectures at UC Berkeley, made this the frame of his 2026 AI Engineer World's Fair talk[Why Agentic Systems Need Ontologies](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Sir59K8ZDPU) . In the talk he lists the three ways a loop goes wrong: it can break, it can drift, and it can cost you money. One of his slides, as[Latent Space reported](https://latent.space/p/ontologies-agentic-systems/) , describes the target shape as a bounded set of rules around an unbounded loop.


That is the whole design in one line. The loop stays creative. The rules stay fixed. The rules are the ontology.


Unbounded loops are not a hypothetical risk either. A July 2026 study,[When Agents Do Not Stop](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01641) , scanned **6,549 agent repositories** and confirmed **68 infinite-loop failures across 47 projects** , describing the mechanism as an agent repeatedly calling models, tools, or handoffs "when the feedback path is not effectively bounded," producing cost exhaustion, runaway context growth, and **repeated external side effects.** That last consequence is the one that reaches customers: a loop that sends the same email nine times is not a billing problem.


### One writer, many advisors


There is a related lesson from the multi-agent debate that took a year to resolve, and it is worth borrowing whole.


In June 2025, Cognition published[a widely-read argument against multi-agent systems](https://cognition.com/blog/dont-build-multi-agents) , on the grounds that "actions carry implicit decisions, and conflicting decisions carry bad results." In April 2026 the same author[revised the position](https://cognition.com/blog/multi-agents-working) with a sharper conclusion: multi-agent systems work best "when writes stay single-threaded and the additional agents contribute intelligence rather than actions."


That is the **single-writer principle** , and it is the ontology argument arriving from a completely different direction. Multiple agents can read, analyze, and propose. Exactly one path commits. Every additional writer is another boundary, and boundaries are where the reflections come from.


Loop design Stop condition Cost behavior


Unbounded self-correction None Grows without limit; quality can degrade


Fixed retry count Attempt number Bounded, but retries are uninformed


**Validation-gated retry** **A rule passes, or a person takes over** **Bounded and informative**

## Should Relationships Be First-Class?


Yes, and this is the cheapest high-value change on the list. When two records refer to each other, **store the reference as a stable ID** , never as a duplicated display name.


Name-based links break the moment a name changes, and they break silently. "Acme Corp" becomes "Acme Corporation" after a rebrand, and every agent that matched on the string now finds nothing, reports nothing found, and carries on. Nothing errors. The data is simply wrong from that point forward.


An agent reading that structure can answer "which invoices belong to this account" by **following references** , which either resolves or fails loudly. An agent reading a flat table of text has to guess, and guessing produces answers that look right.


The discipline is three rules long:


- Prefer a real relationship field over a text field containing a name.
- Prefer a stable ID over any human-readable label.
- Prefer an explicit parent-child link over inferring hierarchy from indentation or naming conventions.


You do not need every noun in your business to become an entity, and you do not need every relationship to become a graph edge. Preserve the connections some workflow actually traverses.

The vendor landscape sorted itself out considerably in 2026. Here is what each player actually does, so you can tell which problem they solve.


Player What it actually is Best fit


**Palantir Foundry Ontology** Object types, link types, and governed action types; agents act only through actions The reference model for governed agent writes


**Microsoft Fabric IQ** Ontology as a first-class item over OneLake, in preview across Microsoft's agent surfaces Teams already standardized on Fabric


**Neo4j** Graph database moving ontologies to first-class with native schema enforcement Genuine multi-hop graph questions


**Zep / Graphiti** Temporal knowledge graph where every fact carries a validity window Agent memory that must expire cleanly


**Cognee** Open-source graph-native memory engine with an extract, cognify, load pipeline Self-hosted agent memory


**Cube** Governed measures and dimensions selected before SQL is written Analytics agents on the read path


**dbt Semantic Layer** Metrics defined once, exposed through APIs and an MCP server Warehouse-centric metric consistency


**TypeDB** Strongly-typed database with inference in the schema Rule-heavy domains, if you accept its query language


**[Apache Ossie](https://ossie.apache.org/)** (incubating) Vendor-neutral semantic spec, announced September 2025 as Open Semantic Interchange, spec published January 2026, in the Apache Incubator since mid-2026, still pre-1.0 Avoiding lock-in across the above


Two structural observations are worth more than the table itself.


**Palantir's action types are the load-bearing idea in the whole category.** Palantir splits its Ontology into semantic elements, which model what exists, and what it calls **kinetic** elements, which model what can be done. Chief Architect Akshay Krishnaswamy put the split memorably in 2024: *"If the data elements in the Ontology are 'the nouns' of the enterprise ... then the actions can be considered 'the verbs.'"*


Two details make this more than branding. Actions are **granularly permissioned** , so an analyst may open an investigation while only a manager group may close one, which is the same permission model a human operator faces. And there is a **Validate Action** API that evaluates a proposed change against its parameters and submission criteria and returns valid or invalid **without executing it** . That is a dry run for a write, exposed as a first-class endpoint.


In their agent tooling, an LLM's ability to change state is expressed as a bounded set of those action types, each of which can be configured to run automatically or only after user confirmation. Krishnaswamy's framing of that choice is the honest one: organizations should *"surgically choose which trusted, well-worn AI processes can automatically close the action loop."* Closing the loop autonomously is a per-process opt-in, not a default. Microsoft's Fabric IQ ontology visibly follows the same object, relationship, and action structure.


**Most of the rest are read-path products.** Cube's governance happens before the SQL. dbt's metrics make numbers consistent. Those are real problems and these are good tools, but neither one stops an agent from writing something untrue. If your agents only answer questions, a semantic layer may be all you need. The moment they change state, you need the other half.

## Frequently Asked Questions


What is an ontology in artificial intelligence and why does it matter?


An ontology is an explicit, shared agreement about what things exist in a domain, what is true about them, and how they relate. Tom Gruber's standard definition is an explicit specification of a conceptualization. It matters for AI agents because a language model has no built-in commitment about what your company means by Customer, Active, or Overdue. Without that agreement written down somewhere the system can check, every agent invents its own definition on every run, and two agents in the same workspace can disagree without either one being detectably wrong.


Is an ontology the same as a knowledge graph?


No. An ontology is the schema and the knowledge graph is the data. The ontology says a Customer can place an Order and that every Order must reference exactly one Customer. The knowledge graph holds the actual customers and orders as nodes and edges. You can have an ontology with no graph at all, expressed as typed fields or JSON Schema, and you can have a graph with no real ontology, which is usually how graphs turn into a pile of inconsistent edges nobody trusts.


What is an example of an ontology for AI agents?


A support refund workflow is a compact example. The ontology names three things: Customer, Order, and Refund. It states that every Order references exactly one Customer, that Order status is one of paid, shipped, or refunded, that an Order has at most one Refund, and that a payout goes to the Customer and never to a support rep. An agent's proposed refund is checked against those rules before anything is written, so a duplicate refund or an invented status is rejected with the rule that failed.


Do you need to build a full ontology before deploying agents?


No, and trying to is the most common way these projects die. A useful ontology for agents needs five things: what the system remembers, what must be known about each thing, how records connect, what must be true, and what changes through use. That is a one-page artifact you can write in an afternoon for a single workflow. Build only what one real loop needs, then let real usage tell you what is missing. Multi-year enterprise modeling efforts routinely deliver nothing because the domain moves faster than the committee.


Can I just put the schema in the system prompt instead of building an ontology?


Putting the schema in the prompt helps the agent read, but it does nothing at the moment the agent writes. A prompt is advisory. The model can still emit a field that does not exist, a status value outside the allowed set, or a reference to a record ID it invented. The difference between a prompt-described schema and a real ontology is that the second one is enforced by something that can reject a bad write. Prompts shape probability; validation changes outcomes.


How does an ontology reduce AI hallucination?


It converts a class of hallucination into a caught error. If the agent invents a customer ID, an ontology that requires every order to reference an existing customer turns that invention into a failed reference check instead of a corrupted record. It does not stop the model from generating something wrong. It stops the wrong thing from becoming true in your system, which is the failure that actually costs money.


Do I need a graph database to build an AI ontology?


No. A graph database is one storage choice, not a requirement. The three things an ontology must supply are typed entities, explicit relationships by stable ID, and constraints that can reject an invalid write. Typed fields in a database, a JSON Schema on a tool call, or a Pydantic model all satisfy that. Reach for a graph engine when your questions are genuinely about multi-hop paths, such as fraud rings or dependency chains, not because the word ontology implies one.


Do AI agents need a knowledge graph, or is vector search enough?


Vector search is good at finding text that resembles your question and bad at guaranteeing that a specific record exists or that two records are genuinely linked. It returns similarity, not truth. For questions like which invoices belong to this account, similarity is the wrong tool, because a near-miss is indistinguishable from a hit. Most production systems use both: vectors to find candidate context, explicit typed relationships to confirm identity before acting on it.


What is the difference between an ontology and a semantic layer?


A semantic layer is usually a read-path product from the analytics world that defines governed metrics and dimensions so queries return consistent numbers. An ontology is broader and includes the write path: what actions are permitted, what must remain true after a change, and how entities relate. In practice a semantic layer answers what does revenue mean, while an ontology also answers whether this agent is allowed to mark this order refunded and what has to be true for that to be valid.


How do you avoid boiling the ocean when designing an ontology?


Start from one workflow that already hurts, not from the org chart. Write down only the entities that workflow touches, the fields it reads or writes, the links it depends on, and the rules that must hold when it finishes. Ship it, then extend it when real usage reveals a gap. The test for whether an entity belongs is whether some agent or automation needs to act on it, not whether it exists in the business.


How should you bound an AI agent loop?


Give every loop a stop condition before you give it autonomy. A defensible default is one plan, one execution attempt, one corrective retry when validation fails, then a handoff to a person. Unbounded self-correction is not free improvement: research has found that language models asked to revise their own reasoning without external feedback often make correct answers worse, while every extra pass costs tokens and latency.


Do I need to be a developer to use an ontology with AI agents?


No. In a workspace tool, the ontology is expressed as ordinary product surfaces: typed fields with fixed options, links between records, and permissions that decide who can change what. Taskade builds this shape automatically when you describe an app in plain language, so the structure the agents share is the same structure you see and edit, with no modeling language to learn.

## The Shortest Version of a Long Idea


Smith did not discover new physics. Oliver Heaviside had written the equations sixty years earlier, and engineers could already calculate the right answer with enough slide rule and enough patience. What Smith did was change the representation until the answer became **visible** , and an industry that had been guessing could suddenly see where to go.


The agent version of that move is not a new model. It is writing down what your system already believes, clearly enough that a machine can check a proposed change against it before the change becomes real. Every serious pattern in this article reduces to the same instruction: **treat agent output as a proposal, not a command.**


The organizations getting this right in 2026 are not the ones with the largest models. They are the ones that stopped trying to make the guess perfect and started making the boundary honest.
